metadata.title: Teaching for near transfer: Is maths instruction aimed at schema formation and abstraction associated with pupils' ability to answer unfamiliar maths questions?

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2019 4th-grade mathematics data pooled across 47 participating countries, with a complex multistage sampling design (schools selected with probability proportional to size; classes sampled within schools). To account for this design, the authors apply TIMSS student (senate) weights throughout the analysis and use Jackknife replication weights for variance estimation, as recommended for TIMSS analyses. The analytic sample is restricted to pupils’ responses to mathematics items that are off-curriculum (novel/unfamiliar) for the main outcome, and the near-transfer question-level analyses further restrict to pupils for whom each specific item is off-curriculum. The manuscript does not report any additional weight variable names beyond describing senate weights and Jackknife replication; therefore, the weighting strategy is implemented via the TIMSS-supplied weights rather than custom reweighting.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are constructed as percent-correct scores on off-curriculum (novel/unfamiliar) mathematics questions and, in the near-transfer analyses, as item-level binary correctness. These are not PV-based cognitive achievement scores from TIMSS (the authors explicitly compute percent correct using observed administered items rather than using IRT/PV imputation). Missing-data handling is only described at a high level (“Missing flags are used to account for the small amount of missing covariate data”) without specifying whether covariates were imputed, deleted, or otherwise treated, so the exact missing-data method is not transparent.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TIMSS 2019 4th-grade mathematics data pooled across all participating countries (47). For the primary “general transfer” outcome, the dependent variable is the percent of off-curriculum (novel/unfamiliar) mathematics questions answered correctly, and the model is estimated on pupils’ responses to those off-curriculum items; on-curriculum (familiar) percent-correct is included as a control in some specifications. For the near-transfer analyses, each specific mathematics item is analyzed separately: the sample is restricted to pupils for whom that item is off-curriculum (unfamiliar), and the model includes the percent correct on curriculum (familiar) items within the same content domain as an additional control. The authors note that missing covariate data are handled via missing flags for a small amount of missing covariate information.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Mathematics (pooled across 47 countries) — off-curriculum items
main_findings.target_variable: Novel/unfamiliar mathematics achievement (percent correct on off-curriculum items)
main_findings.performance_metrics: OLS regression (M1–M3): coefficients for teaching for transfer scale are small (<1 percentage point per 1 SD) and not statistically significant at 5% once on-curriculum performance is controlled (M3). R-squared ranges from 0.244 to 0.396 across specifications.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Mathematics data pooled across 47 countries, the study leveraged the Teaching for transfer scale and percent correct on curriculum questions to predict novel/unfamiliar mathematics achievement (percent correct on off-curriculum items), finding that frequent schema-oriented teaching practices show little to no association with pupils’ performance on unfamiliar items. This indicates that, in authentic primary classrooms, self-reported instructional approaches aligned with schema formation and abstraction may not translate into measurable near transfer to off-curriculum mathematics tasks, though the study is correlational and may be limited by measurement error in teacher reports.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Mathematics (pooled across 47 countries) — item-level off-curriculum questions
main_findings.target_variable: Near transfer within mathematics domains (probability of correct response to off-curriculum items)
top_predictors: Percent correct on curriculum questions within same domain
main_findings.performance_metrics: Logistic regression (Eq. 2): for the teaching-for-transfer scale, the association is not robust; in the pooled all-countries models, the teaching-for-transfer scale coefficient is significant in M1 (Beta=0.730, SE=0.155) but becomes near-zero and non-significant in M3 (Beta=0.006, SE=0.108) after controlling for percent correct on curriculum questions. In the seven focus countries subset, coefficients are also small and not consistently significant across specifications; R-squared ranges from 0.071 to 0.442 depending on specification.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 Mathematics data pooled across 47 countries, the study leveraged the Teaching for transfer scale and within-domain percent correct on curriculum questions to predict near transfer (probability of correct responses to off-curriculum items), finding that any apparent association largely disappears once pupils’ familiar-domain performance is controlled. This indicates that schema-oriented instructional practices, as measured by teacher self-reports, do not show clear evidence of improving near transfer to unfamiliar mathematics items within specific content domains, suggesting that curriculum alignment and/or other mechanisms may be more important for transfer than these reported practices.

data.outcome_summary: This study uses TIMSS 2019 Grade 4 mathematics data from 47 countries (280,083 pupils; 16,050 teachers) to test whether teacher-reported instructional practices aligned with schema formation and abstraction are associated with pupils’ near transfer to off-curriculum (unfamiliar) mathematics items. The primary outcome is percent correct on off-curriculum items, modeled with OLS specifications that include country fixed effects and TIMSS senate weights with Jackknife clustered standard errors by school. Across models, coefficients for the Teaching for transfer scale are small (generally <1 percentage point per 1 SD) and are not statistically significant at 5% once on-curriculum performance is controlled (R-squared up to 0.396). Near-transfer question-level logistic regressions similarly show that any initial association with unfamiliar items largely vanishes after controlling for within-domain familiar performance. The results are correlational and rely on self-reported teaching measures, so measurement error and the lack of causal identification limit policy conclusions.
